title: Introduction to Security
subtitle: 20 questions across physical, logical, wireless, malware, hardening, and data security

questions.q: Which authentication factor category does a fingerprint scanner represent?
questions.note: Biometrics (fingerprint, iris, facial recognition) are classified as 'something you are' — an inherence factor tied to a physical characteristic of the person.

explain.correct: Fingerprints are a biometric trait — a physical characteristic of your body — making them an inherence factor ('something you are').
wrong: Something you know includes passwords and PINs — knowledge the user memorizes, not a physical trait.
Something you have includes smart cards and hardware tokens — physical objects a user possesses, not a body characteristic.
Something you do (behavioral biometrics like typing rhythm) is a subcategory sometimes listed separately, but fingerprints are definitively 'something you are,' not a behavior.

questions.q: A security door with two interlocking doors that only allows one person through at a time is called a:
questions.note: A mantrap, also called an access control vestibule, uses two interlocking doors to prevent tailgating — only one door opens at a time, trapping any unauthorized follower between them.

explain.correct: A mantrap/access control vestibule is specifically designed to stop tailgating by requiring each person to be authenticated before the second door opens.
wrong: A Faraday cage blocks electromagnetic signals — it has nothing to do with door-based physical access control.
Bollards are concrete or metal posts that stop vehicles from ramming a building; they do not control person-level entry.
CCTV is a detective control that records activity; it does not physically prevent tailgating at a door.

questions.q: What type of security control is CCTV camera surveillance?
questions.note: CCTV is a detective control because it identifies and records security events after or as they occur. A deterrent control (like a visible camera sign) discourages behavior; CCTV itself detects it.

explain.correct: CCTV detects incidents by recording them, making it a detective control — it identifies what happened rather than stopping it beforehand.
wrong: Preventive controls stop an incident before it happens (e.g., a locked door). CCTV does not block entry.
Corrective controls restore systems after an incident (e.g., restoring from backup). CCTV does not remediate damage.
Deterrent controls discourage bad behavior (e.g., a 'You are on camera' sign). The camera itself is detective; the warning sign is the deterrent.

questions.q: Why is FM-200 (clean-agent gas) preferred over water sprinklers in a server room?
options: FM-200 is cheaper and easier to install than sprinklers
Water sprinklers trigger faster than any gas system
FM-200 suppresses fire without damaging electronic equipment
Water sprinklers are banned by fire code in data centers
questions.note: Clean agents like FM-200 (HFC-227ea) suppress fire by removing heat or oxygen without leaving residue or water — preventing the water damage that would destroy servers and storage.

explain.correct: FM-200 is a clean agent that suppresses fire without water or conductive residue, protecting sensitive electronic equipment from secondary damage.
wrong: Clean-agent systems are significantly more expensive than sprinklers; cost is not the reason for their use in data centers.
Water sprinklers do not inherently trigger faster; response time depends on the detector type, not the suppression medium.

Water sprinklers are not universally banned by fire code in data centers; pre-action sprinkler systems are actually used in some facilities. The preference for clean agents is about equipment protection, not code prohibition.

questions.q: In the correct order of access control, which step must happen FIRST?
questions.note: Authentication (verifying identity) must always precede authorization (granting access rights). You cannot grant permissions to an unverified identity.

explain.correct: Authentication verifies identity first — the system must confirm WHO you are before it can decide WHAT you are allowed to do (authorization).
wrong: Authorization grants resource permissions, but it is step two — the system cannot authorize an identity it has not yet verified.
Accountability (audit logging) records actions throughout a session but depends on a verified, authorized identity being established first.
Connecting to a resource is the result of both authentication and authorization completing successfully — it cannot be the first step.

questions.q: A user logs in with a password AND receives a one-time code on their phone. This is Multi-Factor Authentication because:
options: Two passwords are always stronger than one password
It combines two DIFFERENT factor categories (know + have)
The phone is encrypted, adding a second security layer
Using a phone number as a second password counts as MFA
questions.note: MFA requires at least two factors from DIFFERENT categories: something you know (password), something you have (phone receiving OTP), or something you are (biometric). Two passwords from the same category is not MFA.

explain.correct: The password is 'something you know' and the phone OTP is 'something you have' — two distinct factor categories, which is the definition of MFA.
wrong: Two passwords are both 'something you know' — the same category. MFA specifically requires factors from DIFFERENT categories, so this would be 2-step verification of a single factor type, not MFA.
Phone encryption is a device security feature, not an authentication factor category. The factor is the possession of the phone (something you have), not its encryption state.
A phone number used as a second password is still 'something you know.' MFA is about different CATEGORIES of factors, not simply having two pieces of information.

questions.q: Which access control model assigns permissions to ROLES, and then assigns users to those roles?
questions.note: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) groups permissions into roles (e.g., 'Nurse,' 'Admin') and assigns users to roles — permissions follow the role, not the individual user.

explain.correct: RBAC defines permissions at the role level (e.g., 'HR Manager' can access payroll). Users inherit those permissions by being assigned to the role — simplifying administration.
wrong: DAC lets resource owners decide who can access their resources — permissions are set by the data owner, not by a centrally managed role structure.
MAC uses system-enforced security labels (e.g., Top Secret, Secret) set by policy — users cannot change access; it is based on classification labels, not roles.
ABAC grants access based on attributes of the user, resource, and environment (e.g., department=HR AND time=business-hours) — more granular than RBAC but not role-centric.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the difference between a VIRUS and a WORM?
options: A virus self-replicates across networks; a worm requires a host file to execute
A worm encrypts files; a virus only deletes files
A virus requires a host file to spread; a worm self-replicates independently
Both are identical — 'virus' and 'worm' are interchangeable terms
questions.note: A virus attaches to and requires a host file (executable, document) to spread. A worm is standalone malware that self-replicates across networks without needing a host file.

explain.correct: A virus cannot spread without attaching to a host file that a user executes. A worm is self-contained and propagates autonomously, often exploiting network vulnerabilities.
wrong: This is exactly backwards. The worm self-replicates independently; the virus needs a host file — not the other way around.
File encryption is the behavior of ransomware, not the defining characteristic of a worm. Worms are defined by self-replication, not by what they do to file contents.
Virus and worm are distinct malware categories with different propagation mechanisms and are not interchangeable in security terminology.

questions.q: Your files are suddenly encrypted and you see a message demanding payment for the decryption key. This is:
questions.note: Ransomware encrypts a victim's files and demands payment (typically cryptocurrency) in exchange for the decryption key. It is one of the most damaging and costly malware types.

explain.correct: Ransomware's defining behavior is encrypting victim data and holding it hostage for payment — the scenario described is the classic ransomware attack pattern.
wrong: A rootkit hides malware and attacker activity from the OS and security tools; it does not encrypt files or demand payment.
A Trojan horse disguises itself as legitimate software to gain entry; it does not typically encrypt files and demand payment as its primary payload.
Spyware silently collects user data (keystrokes, browsing history) and sends it to an attacker; it does not encrypt files or make ransom demands.

questions.q: When responding to a malware infection on a workstation, what should you do FIRST?
options: Run a full antivirus scan while the machine stays online
Isolate the machine from the network
Notify law enforcement before taking any action
questions.note: Isolating (quarantining) the infected machine from the network is the first containment step — it stops the malware from spreading to other systems, receiving new commands from a C2 server, or exfiltrating data.

explain.correct: Network isolation (unplugging from LAN/Wi-Fi) contains the infection immediately — preventing lateral movement, C2 communication, and data exfiltration while investigation proceeds.
wrong: Reimaging destroys evidence needed for investigation and is a recovery step, not the first response action. Isolation and documentation come first.
Keeping an infected machine online while scanning allows malware to continue communicating with attackers, spread to network shares, and potentially spread further.
Law enforcement notification may be appropriate for serious incidents, but it is not the first technical action — containment (isolation) must happen immediately to limit damage.

questions.q: An attacker calls an employee pretending to be the IT help desk and tricks them into revealing their password. This attack is called:
questions.note: Vishing (voice phishing) uses phone calls to manipulate victims into revealing credentials or performing actions. Smishing uses SMS, phishing uses email, and whaling targets executives.

explain.correct: Vishing is social engineering conducted over a voice call — the attacker impersonates a trusted party (like IT) to extract sensitive information verbally.
wrong: Smishing uses SMS text messages to deliver malicious links or requests — the attack vector is text, not a voice call.
Phishing typically uses deceptive emails with malicious links or attachments — the primary vector is email, not a phone call.
Whaling is a phishing attack that specifically targets high-value executives (C-suite). While it can use various vectors, the defining characteristic is the executive target, not the phone medium.

questions.q: An employee holds a secured door open for someone carrying boxes who says they forgot their badge. This is an example of:
questions.note: Tailgating (also called piggybacking) occurs when an unauthorized person follows an authorized person through a secured door, often by exploiting social courtesy. The 'forgot my badge' story is a common pretext used to enable the tailgate.

explain.correct: Tailgating is the physical act of an unauthorized person following an authorized person through a secured entry point. The door-holding behavior is the defining element.
wrong: Pretexting is fabricating a believable scenario to manipulate someone — while the 'forgot my badge' story IS a pretext, the specific security violation being illustrated here is the physical tailgating act.
Whaling targets senior executives via digital attacks; it has no connection to physical door access.
Vishing is a voice-call-based social engineering attack; it does not describe physical unauthorized entry.

questions.q: Which wireless security protocol is considered BROKEN and should never be used?
questions.note: WEP uses a flawed RC4 implementation with static keys that can be cracked in minutes using freely available tools. It has been deprecated and is considered completely broken since the mid-2000s.

explain.correct: WEP's encryption is fundamentally broken — its 24-bit IV (Initialization Vector) is too short and reuses values, allowing statistical attacks that crack the key in minutes.
wrong: WPA3 with SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) is the current gold standard, resistant to dictionary attacks and providing forward secrecy — it is highly secure.
WPA2 with AES-CCMP is the current minimum recommended standard and is considered secure when using a strong passphrase.
WPA2-Enterprise uses 802.1X with a RADIUS server for per-user authentication — it is more secure than WPA2-Personal PSK and is the recommended choice for organizational networks.

questions.q: What makes WPA2-Enterprise more secure than WPA2-Personal (PSK) for a corporate network?
options: WPA2-Enterprise uses a longer encryption key than WPA2-Personal
WPA2-Enterprise authenticates each user individually via 802.1X and RADIUS
WPA2-Enterprise is faster because it skips the handshake process
WPA2-Personal is actually more secure — it uses a shared secret that only employees know
questions.note: WPA2-Enterprise requires each user to authenticate with unique credentials via 802.1X and a RADIUS server. WPA2-Personal uses a single shared passphrase — if it leaks, all users are compromised.

explain.correct: 802.1X/RADIUS in WPA2-Enterprise provides per-user, per-session credentials. Revoking one user does not require changing the passphrase for everyone, and a compromised credential affects only that user.
wrong: Both WPA2-Enterprise and WPA2-Personal use the same AES-CCMP encryption with 128-bit keys. The security difference is in authentication method, not key length.
WPA2-Enterprise does not skip the handshake — it actually adds more authentication steps (EAP exchange with RADIUS). It is more complex, not faster.

WPA2-Personal's shared passphrase is a security weakness: if any employee leaves or the passphrase leaks, it must be changed for all users simultaneously. A shared secret is not more secure in a corporate environment.

questions.q: Why should WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) be DISABLED on a SOHO router?
options: WPS reduces Wi-Fi signal strength by up to 50%
WPS is incompatible with WPA2 and WPA3 encryption
The WPS PIN can be brute-forced in hours due to a design flaw
WPS automatically opens all firewall ports, creating vulnerabilities
questions.note: WPS has a design flaw — the 8-digit PIN is validated in two halves (4+4 digits), reducing the attack space from 100 million to only about 11,000 combinations. Tools like Reaver can brute-force it in hours.

explain.correct: The WPS PIN flaw allows an attacker within Wi-Fi range to brute-force the PIN in hours using tools like Reaver, then recover the WPA2 passphrase — completely bypassing WPA2 security.
wrong: WPS has no effect on signal strength — it is a push-button or PIN-based authentication mechanism, not a radio feature.
WPS was specifically designed to work with WPA2; incompatibility is not the issue. The issue is the PIN's vulnerability to brute force.
WPS does not control or modify firewall rules. It is solely a simplified association/authentication method for connecting devices to a Wi-Fi network.

questions.q: Which Windows feature encrypts the entire hard drive using a key stored in the TPM chip?
questions.note: BitLocker is Windows' full-disk encryption tool. It typically stores the encryption key in the TPM (Trusted Platform Module) chip, so the drive is automatically unlocked on the correct hardware but remains encrypted if removed.

explain.correct: BitLocker encrypts the entire volume (full-disk encryption) and uses the TPM chip to seal the encryption key, ensuring that data is unreadable if the drive is removed and placed in another machine.
wrong: Windows Defender is an antivirus/anti-malware tool — it scans for and removes threats but does not encrypt the disk.
UAC (User Account Control) prompts for administrator consent before allowing privilege elevation — it is an access control feature, not disk encryption.
AppLocker controls which applications are allowed to run (application whitelisting) — it does not encrypt disk contents.

questions.q: AppLocker is more secure than traditional blacklisting because:
options: AppLocker uses AI to detect unknown malware in real time
Blacklists are maintained by Microsoft; AppLocker uses community threat feeds
AppLocker whitelists only approved applications — unknown software is blocked by default
AppLocker encrypts each application before execution to prevent tampering
questions.note: Whitelisting (AppLocker) allows only explicitly approved software to run. Blacklisting only blocks known-bad software, leaving zero-day malware and new threats free to execute until added to the list.

explain.correct: Whitelisting inverts the security model — everything is denied by default, and only approved applications are permitted. This blocks unknown malware automatically, unlike blacklisting which must know about a threat first.
wrong: AppLocker does not use AI or behavioral analysis — it enforces rules based on publisher signature, file path, or file hash. Real-time AI detection is a feature of modern EDR tools, not AppLocker.
AppLocker rules are created and managed by the local administrator or Active Directory Group Policy — not by Microsoft or community feeds. Blacklists can also be locally managed.
AppLocker does not encrypt applications. It controls execution permissions using policy rules — if an application is not on the whitelist, it simply cannot run.

questions.q: An organization needs to wipe a batch of old SSDs before disposal. According to NIST SP 800-88, why is degaussing NOT effective for SSDs?
options: Degaussing requires special SSD adapters not widely available
SSDs store data on flash memory chips, not magnetic platters — degaussing has no effect
Degaussing only works on drives larger than 500GB
SSDs are shielded against magnetic fields by their metal casing
questions.note: Degaussing destroys data by applying a powerful magnetic field to demagnetize platters. SSDs use NAND flash memory (electrical charge in floating-gate transistors), which is not affected by magnetic fields. NIST 800-88 recommends Cryptographic Erase or ATA Secure Erase for SSDs.

explain.correct: Flash memory stores bits as electrical charge states in transistors, not as magnetic orientations. A magnetic degausser has no mechanism to alter electrical charge states, leaving SSD data intact.
wrong: There are no standard SSD degaussing adapters because the technology simply does not work on flash memory — the issue is physical incompatibility, not availability of accessories.
Degaussing effectiveness has nothing to do with drive capacity. It is the storage medium type (magnetic vs. flash) that determines whether degaussing works.
The metal casing of an SSD does not significantly shield flash chips from magnetic fields. The real reason degaussing fails is the non-magnetic nature of flash storage itself.

questions.q: A company allows employees to use personal smartphones for work email (BYOD). Which mobile security control keeps corporate data separate from personal apps?
options: Jailbreaking the device to install corporate security tools
Containerization — a managed workspace that isolates corporate data
Disabling the device's lock screen to speed up access
Installing corporate apps directly into the personal app store account
questions.note: Containerization (used by MDM solutions like Microsoft Intune and VMware Workspace ONE) creates an encrypted, policy-controlled workspace on the device. IT can wipe the container without touching personal data.

explain.correct: Containerization partitions the device into a managed corporate space and a personal space — corporate data stays encrypted in the container, and personal photos/apps remain private. IT can remotely wipe only the container.
wrong: Jailbreaking removes the device's OS security sandbox and voids manufacturer support — it dramatically increases security risk and is the opposite of a sound BYOD security control.
Disabling the lock screen removes the primary authentication barrier to the device, exposing both personal and corporate data to anyone who picks it up.

Installing corporate apps under a personal App Store account blends corporate and personal app ecosystems — IT loses management control and cannot enforce policies or remotely wipe corporate data without affecting personal data.

questions.q: What is the FIRST action you should take when setting up a new SOHO (home/small office) router?
options: Enable WPS for easy device setup
Set the Wi-Fi channel to auto-select for best performance
Change the default administrator username and password
Disable the firewall to improve internet speed
questions.note: Default router credentials (often 'admin/admin' or 'admin/password') are publicly documented for every router model. Attackers scan for routers still using defaults. Changing them is the single most important first hardening step.

explain.correct: Default credentials are publicly listed in manuals and vendor databases. Leaving them unchanged means anyone on your network (or who gains access) can take full administrative control of your router.
wrong: WPS should be disabled, not enabled — its PIN has a known brute-force vulnerability that can compromise the entire Wi-Fi network in hours.
Channel selection is a performance optimization, not a security hardening step — it has no bearing on protecting the router from unauthorized access.
Disabling the firewall removes the router's primary defense against unsolicited inbound traffic. It does not meaningfully improve internet speed and creates serious security exposure.
